Oracle Corporation (NYSE:ORCL) closed at $134.47 on October 15. The stock returned -24.60% over the last 6 months, compared with a 15.4% return for the Insider Monkey Billionaire Index and 11.4% for the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust.

Oracle sells database software and, increasingly, the computing power that runs other companies' artificial intelligence work. The second business is newer, far more expensive to build, and can be the reason the shares have behaved the way they have. The stock has lost 53.84% of its value over the past year. Even so, 80% of the analysts covering it still rate it a buy, and their median target sits 78.48% above today's price, per CNN.

READ ALSO: 10 Cheap Stocks to Buy for High Returns in 2026

Oracle (ORCL) Has Fallen 54% and 80% of Analysts Still Say Buy. Why?
What the Analysts Are Looking At:

The business is still growing quickly. Revenue in the most recent quarter grew by almost a third and earnings grew faster still. Nothing in those figures explains a share price down by more than half.

What analysts are weighing is the order book. Oracle has signed contracts to supply computing capacity far into the future, and those commitments now stand at $638 billion against annual revenue a fraction of that size.

Oracle carries the widest gap of any name in our 10 Most Promising Technology Stocks to Buy Right Now. To see what else made the list, click HERE.

What the Market Is Looking At:

Those contracts have to be built before they can be billed. Oracle's own cash flow statement shows $75.66 billion of capital spending over the past year against $46.94 billion of cash generated from operations. The company is paying out far more than it takes in.

The money is being borrowed, on a scale that has left Oracle with a different sort of balance sheet from the one it carried before this buildout began. So the disagreement is not really about whether the orders exist. It is about what they cost to fulfil, and whether the returns on all that spending arrive before the borrowing becomes a problem.

DON'T MISS: 10 Most Undervalued Quality Stocks to Invest In

Two Ways to Read the Same Company:

The shares trade at 17.76 times what analysts expect next year. For a business growing at this rate, neither that nor the 22.66 times what it earned over the past year is demanding, which is what makes the share price so strange.

The two sides are not disagreeing about the facts. They are pricing different ones. One is pricing the contracts Oracle has won. The other is pricing the cash going out the door to service them. Both are looking at the same company, and neither is obviously wrong.

Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) stock was near $130 as of this writing, about 60% off its record close at $328.33 on Sept. 10, 2025. Shares are down 33% this year, but the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) returned about 13% through September.

A fall this sharp makes the stock tempting, and on earnings it's arguably cheap.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

But I think Oracle's cash flow statement matters more over the next few years. The cloud giant is spending more on its artificial intelligence (AI) build-out than its business takes in, and it plans to spend even more this fiscal year.

My prediction is that Oracle stock trails a fund tracking the S&P 500 from now through 2030.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

The spending is still climbing

Oracle's spending already topped its cash last fiscal year (the company's fiscal years end May 31). Capital expenditures were $55.7 billion in fiscal 2026, while operating cash flow grew 54% to $32.0 billion. That put free cash flow at negative $23.7 billion.

The pace keeps rising. Quarterly capital expenditures climbed over most of fiscal 2026, from $8.5 billion in the first quarter to $18.6 billion in the third, before slipping to $16.5 billion in the fourth. Then spending surged to $28.5 billion in the fiscal first quarter of 2027 (the quarter ended Aug. 31, 2026), more than triple the year-ago total.

For the full fiscal year, management is still guiding for capital expenditures of $90 billion to $95 billion. Customers will fund part of that up front. Even net of customer prepayments and timing effects, though, Oracle plans to spend as much as $70 billion this fiscal year. On the same basis, it spent around $48 billion in fiscal 2026.

The prepayments didn't close the gap in fiscal Q1, either. Operating cash flow surged 184% year over year to $23.1 billion, lifted by $11.4 billion in customer prepayments. Free cash flow was still negative $5.4 billion, the sixth straight quarter below zero.

When does the cash come back?

On Oracle's fiscal Q1 earnings call in September, an analyst asked when the company expects to return to positive free cash flow.

"We have not given a particular time frame on that," chief financial officer Hilary Maxson said. She added that each of Oracle's data center projects "by nature, is a strong free cash flow generating project" once it ramps up.

title: Oracle's Real Growth Story Is Hiding in Its $664 Billion Backlog

Oracle's Real Growth Story Is Hiding in Its $664 Billion Backlog
Will Healy, The Motley Fool

Investors have good reason to be concerned about Oracle (NYSE: ORCL) stock. The company has borrowed heavily to finance its transformation into an artificial intelligence (AI) cloud stock. Moreover, much of its backlog depends on OpenAI, a company that has not performed to expectations financially.

Despite that concern, investors may take comfort in the company's considerable backlog. Even if OpenAI does not perform to expectations, that backlog could still drive Oracle's growth story, and here's how.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: The Motley Fool.
The state of Oracle today

Indeed, Oracle's growth story is likely hiding in the company's $664 billion backlog.

To serve its customers, Oracle has accumulated more than $125 billion in debt to finance the infrastructure needed to meet the demand for its AI cloud services. Since Oracle has a book value of around $67 billion, that debt places significant strain on the company's balance sheet, sparking concern that it could derail its AI cloud ambitions.

Furthermore, yields on some of its corporate bonds have risen above 8%. While that does not compare to the 15% bond yields of a neocloud company like CoreWeave, it has sparked investor concern.

Additionally, nearly half of that is the $300 billion deal it made with OpenAI. Investors have become increasingly skeptical about whether it can afford to honor its agreement with Oracle.

But Oracle has a tremendous backlog without OpenAI. That backlog grew by $209 billion over the previous 12 months, approximately two-thirds the size of its OpenAI deal. Such improvements increase the likelihood that it can monetize its AI investments with or without OpenAI.

Investors can also take comfort in the fact that its revenue for the first quarter of fiscal 2027 (ended Aug. 31) was over $19 billion. That was 30% higher than the year-ago level, and nearly all of that growth came from its cloud segment.

Despite rapidly rising interest expenses, net income in fiscal Q1 was almost $4.8 billion, a 63% yearly increase. Hence, at least for now, the company continues to profit from its AI investments.

Furthermore, it differs from CoreWeave in one key respect. Although an AI downturn would almost certainly bring significant pain, investors should not overlook Oracle's non-cloud segments. Even though they are now slow-growth businesses, they keep the company profitable and could serve as a stabilizing force during a downturn.

As the outgoing week demonstrated, SK hynix Inc. (NASDAQ:SKHY) is one of the most important stocks in the market. The shares are down by more than 16% over the past five days as investors reacted rather violently to a slate of worrying news regarding the ongoing AI buildout. One major report came in the form of remarks by CXMT President, Dr. Cao Kanyu, who claimed that his firm had progressed in a key memory fabrication technology. Cramer tweeted about the movement in the shares:

"High level of fear would normally be attractive. But you have to find buyers of Coreweave bonds, Oracle common stock and SK Hynix, of course. The latter is the epicenter of fear because the Kospi is still up more than 50% so lots of people under water

"SK Hynix still in charge

The violent reaction in the shares points towards the debate surrounding SK hynix, which relates to the demand for AI chips. It, along with Samsung and Micron, is a key player in the high bandwidth memory (HBM) industry. HBM chips are key for AI chip development, and the surging demand led the firm to post a 257% annual revenue growth in its second quarter. The top line growth was accompanied by an equally strong bottom line growth as SK hynix's operating profit jumped by 557% annually.

Jim Cramer Sees a Telling Change in Broadcom’s (AVGO) Stock

With memory chips typically thought of being a cyclical commodity, SK hynix also confirmed during its earnings that it had long term supply agreements with 10 customers to hint at a secular business unperturbed by cyclical fluctuations.

Yet, while management and the bulls assert secularity, the forward P/E ratio of 5.4x still reflects cyclicality which was also bolstered by a recent report from Counterpoint Research that outlined that it expected DRAM memory chip prices to drop by 23% in 2028 over 2027. While China's CXMT might be unable to compete with SK hynix in the HBM market in the short term, other reports have suggested that the firm might experience HBM4 disruptions as some of its equipment orders had slipped into 2027 from H2 2026. And, even though SK hynix manufactures high end memory chips, it didn't make it on our list of 10 Most Promising Technology Stocks to Buy Right Now. However, another memory manufacturer did.

As for Cramer, the recent share price dip came after the CNBC TV host had warned in August that "we will rue the day we let this Monster into our markets." While he praised the firm's business, factors unrelated to the fundamentals drove the viewpoint. Oracle is pushing ahead with heavy AI infrastructure spending, backed by a US$664b cloud backlog and strong Oracle Cloud Infrastructure growth, while funding a large portion through customer prepayments, supplier financing and planned debt raises.

Rising credit default swap spreads, record borrowing costs and delays around Project Jupiter and related power infrastructure put Oracle's execution risk and free cash flow strain in sharp focus, even as it rolls out AI-first offerings like NetSuite QuickStart and deepens cloud security collaborations.

We will look at how Oracle's investment narrative holds up when aggressive AI data center CapEx meets rising funding and execution risk.

Spot opportunities beyond Oracle by scanning hand picked 55 AI infrastructure stocks that are riding the same AI data center and cloud infrastructure wave, which is now under intense funding and execution scrutiny.

Oracle Investment Narrative Recap

To own Oracle today, you need to believe the firm can turn its large AI cloud backlog into profitable usage while absorbing heavy near-term spending and higher funding costs. The key short-term swing factor is execution on AI capacity, including Project Jupiter and other data centers, so that GPU and data center utilization stays tight against US$664 billion of remaining obligations.

The biggest risk is that AI infrastructure build accelerates faster than actual workloads. This scenario could leave Oracle with cash burn, higher interest expenses and credit concerns before contracts ramp. Recent security, marketplace and client wins are helpful for the story, but they do not yet change the fact that execution and free cash flow timing remain the primary pressure points.

The Marvell, Microsoft and Oracle hardware security module working group inside the Open Compute Project is the announcement that most directly intersects with the current AI buildout narrative. It ties Oracle's infrastructure plan to a push for standardized, FIPS 140-3 Level 3 security at the server layer. This matters if customers are signing multi-year AI contracts that expect tight key management.

For investors, this HSM effort feeds into the same catalyst that underpins the broader thesis. Oracle is attempting to position OCI as both high performance and highly secure for AI workloads, from OpenAI-scale tenants to large enterprises. That supports the idea that the large backlog can be used efficiently, while still leaving funding structure, interest costs and project timing as the main operational watchpoints.

When investors think about cloud computing, Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOGL)(NASDAQ: GOOG) and Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) are often the first names that come to mind. But Oracle (NYSE: ORCL) is also making a strong push into AI infrastructure, and its rapidly growing cloud business offers another way to ride the AI boom.

With $5,000 to put to work today, investors may find Oracle a more compelling cloud choice than either of those giants. The reason starts with how fast its cloud business is growing.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
This database giant is becoming a major force in AI cloud

Oracle may be best known for its database software, which businesses use to store and manage critical information. These days, that established business is laying the foundation for a much bigger opportunity: supplying the cloud infrastructure that other companies need to develop and run AI models.

Oracle's cloud infrastructure business is already seeing solid growth, with revenue climbing 121% to $7.4 billion in its most recent quarter. That suggests its cloud business is becoming an important growth engine rather than simply an extension of its traditional software business.

Its massive backlog, meanwhile, provides a longer runway for growth. Oracle's remaining performance obligations (RPO) reached a record $664 billion, up $209 billion year over year. RPO represents contracted revenue that has not yet been recognized, giving investors a clearer view of the company's future revenue.

That means Oracle is seeing surging demand from customers that need cloud capacity for AI training, applications, and inference. Still, that demand isn't limited to one type of customer, and Oracle is positioning itself to capture several parts of that market.

But with competition picking up, the next question is how Oracle is setting itself apart from the biggest names in the cloud business.

Oracle has a different advantage from its larger cloud rivals

Microsoft Azure and Alphabet's Google Cloud compete across broad cloud ecosystems. However, Oracle's opportunity is somewhat different: it has the luxury of combining its established database business with cloud infrastructure designed for demanding enterprise workflows.

That matters because companies wouldn't want to rebuild their IT systems every time a new AI model arrives. Oracle's database expertise helps here, allowing companies to integrate AI into the systems and data they already rely on without disrupting operations.

title: AI Debt Warning Signs Are Piling Up: Why Bond Markets Are Getting Nervous About AI Infrastructure Spending
detail:
AI Debt Warning Signs Are Piling Up: Why Bond Markets Are Getting Nervous About AI Infrastructure Spending
Johnny Rice, The Motley Fool
Fri, October 16, 2026 at 3:15 PM MST 4 min read
CRWV
ORCL
NVDA

Trading disclosure

The artificial intelligence (AI) boom has a bit of a problem: someone has to pay for it. Despite soaring sales, the costs are still far ahead of the revenues, and more and more companies are turning to the debt market to fund the gap and continue the AI build-out.

But as companies borrow more to build their data centers and fill them with advanced chips, investors are getting nervous about when they'll see a return -- or if they will. This week, that fear has shown up in the bond market where yields are spiking, and the cost to insure the debt against default has reached record levels for companies like CoreWeave and Oracle.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

CoreWeave's lenders are getting nervous

The turbulence was rough enough for Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to step in to try to reassure investors, telling investors that CoreWeave's "financial strength is improving every day." Despite his insistence, the company's bond prices have plummeted; some were trading around 80% of face value, firmly in "distressed" territory. Rates are spiking too, with its October 2031 bond yield reaching 16%.

Jensen Huang. Image source: Getty Images.

Perhaps the clearest sign of bond investor unease was the jump in the five- year credit default swaps (CDS) spread -- basically the cost to insure CoreWeave debt against default -- which reached a record high of about 1,195 basis points. In simple terms, that means it would cost an investor $119,500 a year to insure $1 million in CoreWeave debt.

Oracle's borrowing comes under scrutiny

While CoreWeave took the brunt of it, Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) was not spared either. On Thursday, its five-year CDS spread was nearing 300 basis points, a record for the company.

Oracle's notes due in November 2032 were yielding 7.24% on Wednesday. This is coming just on the heels of a recent credit rating downgrade from S&P Global, which now rates Oracle just one notch above speculative or "junk" grade.

The unease extends across the AI trade

Bonds tied to Meta's Hyperion data-center project have fallen, trading around 91 cents on the dollar and yields reaching as high as 7.55% as of late September. CDS spreads have reached above 100 basis points.

SoftBank, a major backer of OpenAI and other AI ventures, saw its five-year CDS spread climb 24 basis points to 424 on Thursday. SpaceX saw its debt-insurance costs rise sharply during the week too.
